title: Record Profits, Falling Stock, And A Target I Cut
description: Record trailing profit, a multiple down by nearly a third, and a position underwater. One of those three is wrong.
body_html:
Table of Contents

  • Where this stands against June

  • The quarter the market misread

  • Thesis scorecard

  • Where the revenue actually came from

  • The new acquisition: the plumbing is nearly done, the cross-sell is barely started

  • Deeper Look Into One Segment

  • The float and the rate question

  • What got worse

  • The model: what I changed and why

  • What the price is assuming

  • How it screens against its peers

  • Verdict

Where this stands against June

I published the the deep dive on 16 June.

Every figure in it was struck before the company split its stock three-for-two on 17 July, the second such split in four months, so carrying the thesis forward means restating the old numbers on today’s share count. On that basis, the June article valued StoneX at $126.73, marked a downside case at $53.49, and the shares changed hands at $77.03.

They trade near $67 as I write. Fifty-two days and one earnings report later, I’m down on the position and the business is worth more than when I wrote it up.

The quarter the market misread

In Q3 2026, volatility moderated from the extraordinary levels of the March quarter, That is precisely the condition my deep dive said would break the earnings power.

Nothing broke. Every headline measure rose and the ROE printed above management’s own hurdle in a period management described as a moderation in volatility. The prior year quarter closed a month before R.J. O’Brien completed, so the comparison flatters the growth rate. Strip out the net operating revenue that R.J. O’Brien and Benchmark contributed and the rest of the business still grew 25%, with a handful of smaller deals sitting inside that figure too.

Earnings fell harder than revenue between March and June because variable compensation and clearing costs fall with revenue while fixed costs don’t. The same arithmetic running the other way is what made the March quarter a record.

SNEX earned $127.9M in the moderation. In all of FY25 it earned $305.9M. Three quarters at this level would clear that entire year.

This is still not a clean read on a calm market. Part of the securities volume growth was due to the onset and continuation of the US and Iran conflict, and management flagged pockets of elevated volatility even while calling conditions moderate. What Q3 shows is what a step down from an extreme costs, and the step was a great deal smaller than the bear case required.

The Street had modelled a considerably softer quarter.

The estimate line keeps getting set at mid-cycle, StoneX keeps clearing it, and the multiple contracts anyway, as though each beat were borrowed from the following quarter.

Thesis scorecard

The deep dive rested on five pillars.

Pillar one, the middle-market gap left by retreating banks. Confirmed. Big banks now set a minimum size of client they will deal with, measured in revenue and in return on the capital they have to tie up. Clients below that line get turned away, and SNEX picks them up. Management said exactly that this quarter when it presented Global Prime.

Pillar two, ROE above 20% compounding retained capital. Confirmed. TTM ROE reached 20.8% and return on tangible equity 28.7%, both against a stated 15% target, and both delivered while the equity base itself grew 77% over two years. Earning a high return on a small book is common. Holding it while the book nearly doubles is the harder trick.

Pillar three, the volatility engine. Evolving. My deep dive argued the cyclicality is a feature because the business grows in calm markets and prints in chaotic ones. Q3 is the first genuine test of the calm half of that claim and it delivered growth. But the sequential give-back was real. I’d now put mid-cycle earnings power nearer this quarter than the record.

Pillar four, free cash flow against the price. Confirmed and improved. Trailing net income now stands at $526.9M against a market capitalization of $7.94B. In June I was underwriting a mid-single-digit cash yield on a $9B price. The price came down, the cash went up, and the yield is materially better than the one I bought.

Pillar five, consolidation. Confirmed. R.J. O’Brien closed on schedule, the large US futures commission merchant integration happened inside the quarter, and cost synergies are tracking to the timetable given a quarter ago.

Four confirmed, one evolving. On the other side of the ledger one bear point has partly materialized and two have faded.

Where the revenue actually came from

Growth is broad. Every product line except foreign exchange and contracts for difference grew against the prior year, and volumes grew across the board on the same single exception. In listed derivatives and securities the rate capture and the volume rose together, so SNEX was paid more per unit while doing more units. That is pricing power rather than a volume grab.

Physical contracts is where the volatility premium concentrated. Precious metals dislocations between delivery locations drove most of that growth, and management was direct that the last two quarters exceeded its own expectations. Those revenues fell 39% from the March record. The 10Q adds a further $6.4M of realized gains on physical inventories carried at the lower of cost or net realizable value, against derivative losses booked in earlier periods, which is a timing item rather than trading performance. That whole line is the part of the earnings base I don’t capitalize, and my forecast reflects it.

Commercial and Institutional carried the quarter, and their margins moved in opposite directions. Institutional gave margin back because pay rose faster than revenue: variable compensation up 88% and fixed pay up 47%, against a 56% revenue gain. Most of that is Benchmark, the investment bank SNEX bought. Investment banks hand their bankers a fixed share of every dollar those bankers bring in, so the revenue arrives already spoken for. Buy the bank and you buy the pay deal with it. Commercial went the other way and widened its margin on the physical and over-the-counter mix.

R.J. O’Brien contributed $187.7M of operating revenue in the quarter and $10.0M of net income. That is a much thinner margin than the group earns, which says the acquired business is still being turned around. It also means the reported growth carries a mix drag that should reverse as the cost saving builds.

On a trailing basis, Commercial and Institutional are close to equal in size and together produce 85% of segment income, with Payments a small high-margin annuity and Retail shrinking. The four balanced legs I described in June are really two large legs, one annuity and one wasting asset. That is a downgrade to the diversification argument.

R.J. O’Brien: the plumbing is nearly done, the cross-sell is barely started

This was the deal that made SNEX the largest non-bank futures commission merchant in the US, and the largest transaction the company has ever done.

On cost, management exited the March quarter at a $32M annualized synergy run rate and exited June at $37M-$38M, tracking to $45M-$46M by the end of the year and the originally announced $50M by the end of the December quarter. Every one of those milestones is the schedule management gave last quarter.

On integration, management moved the vast majority of R.J. O’Brien’s remaining US client migration during the quarter, with the consolidation work on track to be substantially completed later this year. It is close to done rather than done.

On revenue, the CEO declined to attach a number to the cross-sell, saying the firm never guided to revenue synergies because it didn’t want to be bound by a timeline that would push unsuitable products at clients. But at the time of the deal management pointed to revenue synergy potential exceeding the expense synergies. Early wins do exist, mostly platform and physical-hedging capabilities legacy clients are already using. What hasn’t happened at any scale is the over-the-counter and payments cross-sell into the 350 introducing brokers R.J. O’Brien brings, each with underlying clients of their own.

That opportunity sits outside my forecast and outside management guidance, so it is upside I haven’t paid for. The question is what happens if it never arrives. R.J. O’Brien cost $942M and contributed $49.2M of net income over nine months. Annualize that, add the announced cost saving after tax, and the deal earns close to 11% on the purchase price with no revenue synergy at all, though part of that saving already sits inside the contribution. Acceptable on its own, and good if the cross-sell lands.

Global Prime Services

Each quarter SNEX spotlights one business line and this quarter it was Global Prime Services.

This business didn’t exist in any meaningful form eight years ago. It now serves hedge funds, ETF providers, family offices and digital asset managers across five cities, by offering execution, clearing, custody and financing to managers the large prime brokers won’t take.

Prime matters beyond its own revenue because it anchors the client. Once a manager holds assets and finances positions on the platform, selling them foreign exchange, payments, clearing and market making gets much easier. Some clients now come on board across seven products at once.

SNEX holds close to $1.5B in traditional assets for digital asset funds, letting those managers keep fiat and fixed income collateral separate from crypto exposure while financing the traditional side on the same platform. Most incumbents won’t touch that client segment.

The float and the rate question

Interest earned on client balances is the part of the thesis most exposed to the rate cycle, and it grew hard this quarter as the R.J. O’Brien client float landed.

A 100 basis point move in short rates, in either direction, shifts annual net income by close to 9% of trailing earnings. That figure is struck after the hedge book, so it is the exposure that remains rather than the gross one, and it cuts against the position if the Fed eases.

Two things soften it. Management added $750M of two-year swaps during the quarter, taking the hedged position to $2.55B at an average rate of 3.51%, which is why the residual sensitivity is as contained as it is. And client float grew 108% against the prior year with management guiding to high single-digit growth once the acquisition annualizes, so the balance can grow into a lower rate. Working the other way, the ten-year Treasury sits near 4.6% today, above where it was when I built the June model, and that lands in the discount rate rather than the earnings.

What got worse

Four things deteriorated this quarter.

  • Self-Directed/Retail is now a shrinking business. Net operating revenue fell 20% on a trailing basis and segment income fell 39%. In the quarter itself, segment foreign exchange and contracts for difference volumes fell 27%, partly offset by better rate capture. In June I called this the high-octane option in the portfolio. It looks closer to a wasting asset, and I’ve modeled it declining again next year.

  • Payments rate per million sits well below where it was before the XPay platform launched, and the CEO expects the downward trend to continue. XPay, which management put at a fifteenfold capacity increase, opened the business to high-volume low-value bank flow that is accretive in aggregate and dilutive per transaction. The CFO pushed back on the same call, noting rate per million has risen through this year off its first-quarter trough. Both can be true, and the line to watch is whether volume keeps outrunning price.

  • Bad debts rose to $12.6M over nine months vs. $2.3M in the same period last year, most of it in Commercial. The quarter itself recorded a small net recovery, so this isn’t yet a trend. It is exactly the line item that goes wrong first at a clearing firm, and the tail risk I flagged in June hasn’t gone anywhere.

  • The corporate net operating loss more than doubled over nine months as the funding cost of the 2032 notes landed. That drag is now permanent and I’ve modeled it as such.

The model: what I changed and why

The June forecast is obsolete. It had SNEX earning $2,322M of net operating revenue in FY26. Nine months are already in the bank at $2,273.2M.

You can review the full model here.

I rebuilt the forecast from the nine months of actuals with a fourth quarter modeled slightly below the third, on the view that the precious metals dislocation keeps unwinding while Institutional and Payments hold. That lands FY26 net operating revenue at $2,980M, which is 45% growth on the year, and net income at $567M.

I modeled FY27 flat. Commercial declines as the metals windfall reverses, Retail declines again, Institutional and Payments grow, and the net of those four is a year with no growth at all. That is a deliberately unflattering assumption for a business that has compounded at 19% over five years.

Three inputs changed beyond the operating forecast. The risk-free rate moved from 4.2% to 4.6%, lifting the discount rate. The share count moved to the post-split figure of 120.6M. And the cost ratios now reflect what the business actually delivered over nine months rather than what I projected in June. I left the through-cycle ROE at 18% despite a TTM of 20.8%, and I left terminal growth untouched.

The result is a base case of $120 a share and a downside case of $59. Against June the target falls 6% on a like-for-like basis even though earnings are running far ahead of the old forecast. The higher discount rate cuts the equity value, and there are slightly more shares to divide it by.

What the price is assuming

Run the model backwards and ask what $64 already believes. Hold my forecast and an 18% through-cycle ROE, and the price implies the business shrinks 3% a year, in nominal terms, forever. Hold my 4.7% growth rate instead, and it implies a 10% cost of equity, which is the rate you would use on a leveraged cyclical rather than a 0.65-beta business whose earnings rise when markets get violent. Hold both, and it implies a sustainable ROE of 8%, against the 20.8% delivered over the last twelve months.

Each of those is an aggressive assumption on its own, and the price needs one of them to hold. The R.J. O’Brien revenue synergy and a prime brokerage that has compounded at better than 60% a year since 2019 come free on top.

At $64 the shares trade at under 14 times the $4.70 of earnings I expect this fiscal year, against five years in which net operating revenue compounded at 19% and an ROE that has stayed in double digits through a pandemic, a rate shock and a commodity dislocation.

How it screens against its peers

RankedStocks.com puts SNEX at 77 out of 100, in the strong band and the top fifth of US financials.

Outlook is the strongest factor and Sentiment is close behind. Profitability sits mid-band, which understates a business earning 28.7% on tangible equity, because the margin is computed on the gross revenue line.

Valuation and Growth score red for the same reason. When SNEX sells a metal or a crop on behalf of a client, it books the full sale price as revenue and the full purchase price as a cost, and keeps a small fee in between. That makes reported revenue over $150B with almost no margin on it. The screen takes those figures at face value, so it sees a huge company that barely makes money and a revenue line about to shrink. Score the business on what it actually keeps and both figures invert.

SNEX carries the lowest forward operating margin and the steepest forward revenue decline of the eleven names on the table, which makes it look like a business winding down. On net operating revenue, the measure management runs the company on, SNEX earned a 25.2% pre-tax margin over the last nine months and grew 55%.

SNEX has the highest outlook score of the group, and every peer that screens cheaper than it on valuation scores worse on outlook.

Verdict

BUY, target $120.

I bought this company because the market was reading a capital-light intermediary as a thin-margin commodity trader. That misreading has intensified rather than corrected, and the stock is 20% cheaper than when I published it. The quarter that was supposed to break the argument returned 18.4% on equity in conditions management itself called a moderation, and grew 25% before any acquisition contribution.

If this was useful, forward it to someone who still thinks a 14x multiple on a compounder is a value trap.
